questions.q: Which Salesforce API is purpose-built for moving very large data volumes asynchronously, rather than one record per call?
options: SOAP API
Metadata API
Bulk API
Tooling API
questions.explain: Bulk API is designed for large-volume asynchronous data movement, processing records in large batches behind the scenes — the right tool for a nightly sync of hundreds of thousands of records, unlike the REST or SOAP APIs which are built for synchronous, smaller-volume CRUD operations.

questions.q: In API-led connectivity's three-layer model, what is the specific job of a Process API?
options: It sits closest to the backend system and hides that system's implementation details
It orchestrates business logic across one or more System APIs, combining and shaping data to match a business process
It is shaped exactly to a single consumer's UI needs and cannot be reused by any other consumer
It handles only authentication and has no role in data orchestration
questions.explain: A Process API sits above System APIs and orchestrates business logic across them — combining data from multiple System APIs and applying business rules — distinct from the System layer below it and the Experience layer above it.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the System/Process/Experience split is the antidote to the N-squared problem from Lesson 3, applied to API design?
options: Because it eliminates the need for any API versioning

Because a System API built once for a backend can support many Process APIs over time, and a Process API can support several Experience APIs, without rebuilding the backend connection for every new consumer
Because it requires every consumer to connect directly to every backend system
Because it removes the need for any authentication between layers
questions.explain: The three-layer split is built for reuse: one System API connection can serve many Process APIs, and one Process API can serve many Experience APIs, avoiding a fresh point-to-point connection for every new consumer that shows up.

questions.q: What problem do Named Credentials solve, architecturally?
options: They eliminate the need for an API gateway entirely
They bundle a callout's endpoint and authentication details into a single reusable reference, so credentials aren't hard-coded and can be rotated or updated in one place
They replace the need for any Apex code in an integration
They are only usable with the Bulk API, not with REST or Apex callouts
questions.explain: Named Credentials centralize where a callout's endpoint and authentication live, so changing a Named Credential once updates every piece of code or Flow referencing it, instead of hunting down hard-coded URLs and credentials scattered across an org.

questions.q: What does External Services add on top of Named Credentials?
options: It lets an admin register an external API by its specification and have Salesforce auto-generate invocable actions that Flow Builder can call declaratively
It replaces Named Credentials entirely and is no longer compatible with them
It is used exclusively for Metadata API operations, not for external callouts
It only works with SOAP-based external APIs, never REST
questions.explain: External Services builds on a Named Credential to register an external API (described via an OpenAPI/Swagger-style specification) and auto-generate Flow-invocable actions, so declarative tools can call individual operations without hand-written Apex callout code.
